memories.content: [task-2/advisor1/structure] Complete the problem framing within the first two sentences so the reader reaches the proposal's central issue before any supporting background.
[task-2/advisor1/structure] Use the first sentence for the concrete problem and the second for its consequence; reserve later sentences for the proposed response.
[task-2/advisor1/structure] Specify the user, context, and interaction to be explored in the primary HCI research question.
[task-2/advisor1/structure] Provide one compact visual summary when proposing an unfamiliar interaction procedure.
[task-2/advisor1/structure] Mark the conditions that move an unfamiliar interaction procedure from one step to the next in its visual summary.
[task-2/advisor1/structure] Present the master’s research schedule as phased periods for exploration, design, prototyping, and user evaluation.
[task-2/advisor1/structure] Link one reviewable deliverable to each phase of the master’s research.
[task-2/advisor1/structure] Place the gap left by HCI-related research and the proposed design and empirical contributions in close proximity.
[task-2/advisor1/structure] Divide a two-page proposal with short descriptive subheadings so a reader can jump directly to the problem, proposed response, and next steps.
[task-2/advisor1/structure] Give the problem and proposed response their own descriptive subheadings instead of relying only on paragraph transitions.
[task-2/advisor1/structure] Give the next steps and requested support their own descriptive subheading so they remain easy to find on a return visit.
[task-2/advisor1/structure] Place pilot observation or initial prototype results near sentences supporting feasibility claims.
[task-2/advisor1/structure] Readers often decide what a proposal is about from its first two sentences before scanning the rest of the page.
[task-2/advisor1/structure] When setup continues past the second sentence, readers who are skimming often retain the background topic but miss the exact problem being proposed.
[task-2/advisor1/structure] Reuse the same short subheadings in discussion so a reader can return to a section without searching through the whole page.
[task-2/advisor1/structure] Use visible subheadings as a completeness check: an empty or missing section makes an omitted part of the proposal immediately apparent.
[task-2/advisor1/structure] Readers often scan section labels before deciding which paragraph to read closely.
[task-2/advisor1/emphasis] Do not exceed two primary HCI contributions.
[task-2/advisor1/emphasis] Name each design or empirical contribution and present it in a single sentence.
[task-2/advisor1/emphasis] In studies recruiting community participants, emphasize the time burden associated with participation.
[task-2/advisor1/emphasis] In studies recruiting community participants, emphasize the travel burden associated with participation.
[task-2/advisor1/emphasis] HCI reviewers find it difficult to identify primary contributions when named design or empirical contributions exceed two.
[task-2/advisor1/emphasis] Emphasize the core design decisions that formative evaluation will change rather than a polished product demonstration.
[task-2/advisor1/emphasis] Emphasize design principles transferable to other similar interactions as the primary contribution, rather than the performance of a specific prototype.
[task-2/advisor1/emphasis] Formative evaluation creates grounds for modification in subsequent iterations rather than definitively determining the superiority of design alternatives.
[task-2/advisor1/style] Avoid em dashes in the proposal; split the sentence or use more ordinary punctuation instead.
[task-2/advisor1/style] The user tends to place several independently reviewable claims in one long sentence.
[task-2/advisor1/style] Use first-person active voice for choices and commitments owned by the proposal author so responsibility remains explicit throughout the work plan.
[task-2/advisor1/style] Describe prototype operations that have already been implemented and verified as observed states.
[task-2/advisor1/style] Describe prototype operations not yet implemented or evaluated as plans or expectations.
[task-2/advisor1/style] When a commitment is phrased passively, readers may interpret it as uncertainty, evasiveness, or reluctance to take responsibility.
[task-2/advisor1/style] Use “we” only for decisions and commitments the authors control, not for external facts or actions owned by another party.

[task-2/advisor1/style] The user should use one first-person pronoun consistently for the same authorial role and should not alternate between “I” and “we” unless the responsible party actually changes.
[task-2/advisor1/style] The user tends to hide unsettled commitments behind passive phrases such as “will be considered” or “is expected.”
[task-2/advisor1/style] Split proposal prose into short sentences when a sentence contains more than one independently reviewable claim.
[task-2/advisor1/style] Keep one main claim in each sentence so a reviewer can locate and assess it quickly.
[task-2/advisor1/style] The user tends to repeat em dashes when a sentence already contains several clauses.
[task-2/advisor1/style] Repeated em dashes can shift a reviewer’s attention from the proposal’s argument to suspicion that its prose was generated by AI.
[task-2/advisor1/claim-evidence] Attach adjacent evidence or citations to verifiable claims about user behavior or technology effects.
[task-2/advisor1/claim-evidence] Distinguish between results observed in the pilot and expectations to be confirmed in the main user study using different expressions.
[task-2/advisor1/claim-evidence] Do not use verbs that imply proving causation if the design does not support causal inference.
[task-2/advisor1/claim-evidence] For topics with sufficient HCI research evidence, prioritize citing recent comprehensive studies over listing individual cases.
[task-2/advisor1/claim-evidence] Explain how each design choice was derived to address specific user needs.
[task-2/advisor1/claim-evidence] Support each core claim with evidence that directly examined it rather than with indirect summaries.
[task-2/advisor1/claim-evidence] Reviewers first check the direct evidence placed closest to the core claim.
[task-2/advisor1/claim-evidence] Connect the proposed conceptual design principle to at least one observable user behavior.
[task-2/advisor1/claim-evidence] Identify which design judgment—retain, modify, or discard—each piece of evidence from formative evaluation supports.
[task-2/advisor1/claim-evidence] Results from controlled formative studies do not directly prove effects in actual long-term use.
[task-2/advisor1/claim-evidence] The user can have an explanation approved as a conceptual contribution only if it is falsifiable with observable data.
[task-2/advisor1/expression] Use a flow diagram rather than a sequence table when alternate procedural branches lead to different outcomes.
[task-2/advisor1/expression] Draw alternate branches and their resulting outcomes in the same flow diagram so readers can compare them at once.
[task-2/advisor1/expression] The visual fidelity of a prototype may differ from its functional fidelity.
[task-2/advisor1/expression] A flow diagram can make alternate branches and their different outcomes visible in one view.
[task-2/advisor1/expression] HCI reviewers often skim prototype screens and interaction flow diagrams before reading the main text.
[task-2/advisor1/expression] Readers can understand the overall branching shape of a procedure more quickly from a flow diagram than from rows read one at a time.
[task-2/advisor1/expression] Redrawing a branching flow diagram after a procedural change usually takes longer than updating one row in a table.
[task-2/advisor1/expression] Reviewers often inspect the proposal’s main visual before reading the procedural explanation in full.
[task-2/advisor1/terminology] Use the same term throughout the proposal for the same interaction concept or interface element.
[task-2/advisor1/terminology] Use abbreviations only for recurring terms of three or more words.
[task-2/advisor1/terminology] Present the full name and abbreviation together when using an abbreviation for the first time.
[task-2/advisor1/terminology] Prioritize the research role over diagnostic labels or deficits when referring to participants.
[task-2/advisor1/terminology] Reviewers from different subfields struggle to infer undefined abbreviations from context alone.
[task-2/advisor1/terminology] Use the term formative evaluation for studies seeking design modification evidence, and distinguish it from final efficacy judgments.
[task-2/advisor1/terminology] The user can have contribution labels such as principles, models, or guidelines approved only if they align with the abstraction level of the actual deliverables.
[task-2/advisor1/terminology] Design principles describe the relationship between conditions and outcomes rather than serving as instructions that merely replicate a single screen layout.
[task-2/advisor1/methods] Link each HCI research question directly to corresponding user data and analysis procedures.
[task-2/advisor1/methods] In preregistered studies, specify the conditions under which deviations from the plan are permissible.
[task-2/advisor1/methods] In preregistered studies, specify how to record content that deviates from the plan.
[task-2/advisor1/methods] Commit to one exact target number of participants so the schedule, workload, and budget can be checked against the same quantity.
[task-2/advisor1/methods] Specify the interview protocols, recording devices, or log tools used to collect each type of user data.
[task-2/advisor1/methods] Specify whether each type of user data is collected before, during, or after the interaction.
[task-2/advisor1/methods] Readers cannot tell whether the schedule and budget agree when different sections imply different target counts.
[task-2/advisor1/methods] In formative evaluation prototypes, implementation instability exists as an independent cause of task failure alongside design choices.
[task-2/advisor1/methods] If a prototype safety signal occurs during formative evaluation, existing institutional safety procedures take precedence over planned data collection.
[task-2/advisor1/methods] Reviewers judge answerability by tracing the path from each research question to the data and analysis.
[task-2/advisor1/methods] The author of this proposal tends to present implemented feature lists directly as design contributions.
[task-2/advisor1/methods] Calculate the required sessions, facilitator hours, and participant payments from the same exact target rather than from separate rough estimates.
[task-2/advisor1/methods] If recruitment falls below the exact target, state the shortfall explicitly and revise the affected schedule or deliverable.
[task-2/advisor1/methods] Do not use a wide range merely to postpone choosing the quantity that the rest of the proposal must support.
[task-2/advisor1/evaluation] Specify a single representative measure that serves as the criterion for retaining, modifying, or discarding compared design alternatives.
[task-2/advisor1/evaluation] HCI review panels verify whether clear criteria for judging design alternatives are established using the declared primary measure.
[task-2/advisor1/evaluation] Collect process measures to diagnose interaction steps where problems occurred, alongside the primary outcome measure.
[task-2/advisor1/evaluation] Interpret evaluation results as differences between compared design alternatives rather than as success or failure of a single prototype.
[task-2/advisor1/evaluation] Check boundary cases to verify whether the derived design principles retain explanatory power for adjacent situations not included in the comparison.
[task-2/advisor1/evaluation] Controlled evaluation environments do not reproduce time pressure, peer intervention, or voluntary termination conditions found in daily use.
[task-2/advisor1/ethics] Link expected participant burden in each user study task to its corresponding mitigation strategy.
[task-2/advisor1/ethics] Specify the accommodations necessary for participants to access the prototype and research tasks.
[task-2/advisor1/ethics] Specify how accessibility accommodations will be provided during user study sessions.
[task-2/advisor1/ethics] Describe how personal identifiers will be separated from research data immediately after collection.
[task-2/advisor1/ethics] Specify the equipment to be loaned to participants who lack necessary devices.
[task-2/advisor1/ethics] Describe the procedure for returning equipment loaned to participants.
[task-2/advisor1/ethics] HCI ethics reviewers verify that expected burdens and mitigation strategies correspond to each user study task.
[task-2/advisor1/ethics] Inform participants that the formative evaluation prototype is not a finished service.
[task-2/advisor1/ethics] Set an upper limit on cumulative task burden when requesting repeated evaluations from the same participant.
[task-2/advisor1/ethics] The author of this proposal tends to emphasize expected benefits of the prototype over participant burden.

[task-2/advisor1/ethics] In organizations where leaders or institutional staff handle recruitment, recruitment authority and academic or professional evaluation authority may be combined in the same role.
[task-2/advisor1/scope] Define in one sentence the user groups and usage contexts to which the design knowledge does not apply.
[task-2/advisor1/scope] Reviewers judge the generalization boundary of results through explicitly excluded targets and situations.
[task-2/advisor1/scope] Specify user goals, interaction conditions, and technological constraints under which the proposed design knowledge can be transferred.

[task-2/advisor1/scope] Small-scale formative studies can support analytic generalization distinct from statistical representativeness when results are expressed in terms of design conditions and mechanisms.
[task-2/advisor1/scope] The author of this proposal tends to apply design knowledge derived from an accessible sample to a broader user population.
[task-2/advisor1/safety] Specify the order and recipients for reporting serious discomfort during the study.
[task-2/advisor1/safety] Field staff rely on a pre-defined contact sequence when serious discomfort is reported.
[task-2/advisor1/safety] Establish criteria for halting the use of a design alternative if recurring severe errors appear during formative evaluation.
[task-2/advisor1/safety] Do not include a design alternative halted for safety reasons in subsequent evaluation iterations without modification.
[task-2/advisor1/safety] Even in controlled environments, delayed prototype recovery procedures increase session interruption time and alter data collection conditions for the same task.
[task-2/advisor1/feasibility] Mark unverified schedule assumptions as such.
[task-2/advisor1/feasibility] Mark unverified recruitment assumptions as such.
[task-2/advisor1/feasibility] Mark unverified technical assumptions as such.
[task-2/advisor1/feasibility] Clarify which stage of prototype fabrication or user study each requested resource is used for.
[task-2/advisor1/feasibility] Operations reviewers judge feasibility based on the personnel assigned to each procedure.
[task-2/advisor1/feasibility] Operations reviewers judge feasibility based on the equipment assigned to each procedure.
[task-2/advisor1/feasibility] Operations reviewers judge feasibility based on the time allocated to each procedure.
[task-2/advisor1/feasibility] Verify that the planned number of formative evaluation iterations is feasible within the time for prototype modification and recruitment resources.
[task-2/advisor1/feasibility] Include only the minimum functionality required to compare primary design assumptions in the scope of the formative evaluation prototype.
[task-2/advisor1/feasibility] The user's iterative design plan can be judged feasible only if time and personnel are allocated for modifying the prototype between iterations.
[task-2/advisor1/feasibility] Delays in participant recruitment can compress the time available for prototype modification between formative evaluations.
[task-2/advisor1/reproducibility] HCI reviewers find it difficult to assess the reproducibility of results if the prototype version used in the evaluation is not disclosed.
[task-2/advisor1/reproducibility] Record the manipulated and fixed elements of compared design alternatives so that other researchers can reconstruct them.
[task-2/advisor1/reproducibility] Records of formative evaluation decisions enable the reconstruction of connections between raw data, interpretation, and design modifications.
[task-2/advisor1/reproducibility] The user must make it possible to trace which observations each prototype version reflects so the process of deriving design knowledge can be reviewed.
[task-2/advisor1/budget] Keep the total, major cost categories, and one-line estimate basis in the main text so the resource argument can be understood without leaving the proposal.
[task-2/advisor1/budget] Place each major cost beside the activity or deliverable it enables in the main text.
[task-2/advisor1/budget] State the quantity and unit-rate basis for each major cost in the same paragraph that requests it.
[task-2/advisor1/budget] Readers may question a proposed priority when its cost cannot be checked on the same page as the claimed benefit.
[task-2/advisor1/budget] Update the cost sentence whenever the related activity changes so the narrative and requested amount cannot drift apart.
[task-2/advisor1/budget] Accept a denser main-text paragraph when the estimate basis is essential to deciding whether the request is proportionate.
[task-2/advisor1/budget] The user tends to revise the work plan but forget a detached budget table unless the key amount is repeated beside the activity.
[task-2/advisor1/compensation] Calculate user study compensation budgets based on estimated participation burden, combining session time and preparation effort.
[task-2/advisor1/compensation] Compensate for required travel time in face-to-face user studies as well.
[task-2/advisor1/compensation] Compensate for the actual time participants spent in sessions, regardless of research modality.
[task-2/advisor1/compensation] Leave cash payment as an available compensation method for face-to-face studies.
[task-2/advisor1/compensation] If compensation equity is explained, do not require finalizing the payment method at the proposal stage.
[task-2/advisor1/compensation] Apply the same base hourly rate to face-to-face and remote studies if task burden is equal.
[task-2/advisor1/compensation] Participants judge compensation fairness based on the total burden, combining session time with required travel and preparation time.
[task-2/advisor1/compensation] Account in compensation for the burden of rescheduling iterations and returning for multiple formative evaluation sessions.
[task-2/advisor1/compensation] Compensate participants for time already invested even if a session is terminated early due to prototype errors.
[task-2/advisor1/compensation] The author of this proposal tends to exclude preparation burden between sessions when calculating compensation for iterative studies.
[task-2/advisor1/review] Conduct one review prior to submission focusing solely on the validity of user problems, design interventions, and evaluation logic.
[task-2/advisor1/review] Cross-check whether research questions align with the core functions of the prototype.
[task-2/advisor1/review] Cross-check whether evaluation tasks align with representative measures.
[task-2/advisor1/review] Cross-check whether collected evidence aligns with design and operational decisions to be changed.
[task-2/advisor1/review] Verify at the end that user problems, design interventions, user studies, and expected contributions form a coherent logical flow.
[task-2/advisor1/review] HCI reviewers view the validity of design interventions as low if research questions are not linked to prototype functions.
[task-2/advisor1/review] HCI reviewers view the validity of evaluation plans as low if evaluation tasks do not produce representative measures.
[task-2/advisor1/review] HCI reviewers view the practicality of contributions as low if collected evidence cannot change design or operational decisions.
[task-2/advisor1/review] Cross-check at the end whether each research question, formative evaluation data, and design modification judgment are seamlessly connected.
[task-2/advisor1/review] Review whether the application conditions of proposed design principles and boundary cases of failure are presented together.
[task-2/advisor1/review] The user can have contributions reviewed only if prototype outcomes and the transferable design knowledge derived from them are separated.
[task-2/advisor1/review] The scope of observation in controlled formative evaluations does not include long-term adaptation and operational changes in real-world usage contexts.
Place observational evidence or sources adjacent to claims regarding user needs or field effects.
Distinguish at the sentence level between facts already confirmed in the field and predictions to be examined in the user study.
Do not use verbs implying proof of causality if the design does not support causal inference.
Prioritize citations of recent systems and field research in rapidly changing HCI topics.
Explain the user or operational stakeholder needs that each design choice aims to address.
Support each important conclusion with the closest evidence that directly examined it.
Reviewers first check direct evidence placed closest to important conclusions.
Use field cases in which people completed tasks by working around existing tools as evidence for the need for the design.
Distinguish between problems reported by operational stakeholders and those directly observed by the researcher as separate forms of evidence.
Field breakdown logs can reveal both system failures and user adaptive behaviors, including their timing and conditions.
In field sites introducing new systems, formal procedures often coexist with existing manual routines for a period, making it difficult to isolate the effects of single design changes.

analysis.overview: Both frames align on core claim-evidence discipline and calibrated causal language. They preserve context-specific citation guidance, while the reference supplies a broad proposal-development framework and the compared frame adds fieldwork evidence practices and transitional-system cautions.
